decisions.decision: The measured asymmetry, re-read by the coordinator at 9a09ef8. internal/application/service.go:131 reserves quota.ReadTransactionUsage (6,001 reads, 1 write) inside every read transaction and service.go:148 reserves quota.MutationUsage (32 reads, 16 writes) inside every mutation, before the callback can stage anything. internal/store/firestore then settles it: trueUpQuota (store.go:474-497) computes actual = {Reads: len(u.cache), Writes: len(u.values)} and calls quota.Counter.TrueUp before flush() issues any write (store.go:566-568), and countReads (store.go:515-524) feeds that same cache from every query and batch-get path, measured as 13 call sites. internal/store/memory's entire quota implementation is ONE line: ReserveQuota (store.go:167-169) calls u.s.quota.Reserve and nothing ever settles it. quota.DefaultBudget allows 25,000 reads per UTC day, so exactly four read transactions fit in a day on the in-memory adapter and the fifth is refused. internal/quota/quota_test.go:231-246 already documents the figure (worst-case read capacity 4, mutation capacity 625) and that truing up raises it.
decisions.rationale: The consequence is not slowness, it is that a green test on the fast adapter is not evidence about the slow one -- the budget binds at four on one and effectively never on the other, so the two adapters disagree about what a reservation costs, which is precisely non_goals item 3 read as a present-tense defect rather than a prohibition. The scars are already in the tree and were measured: internal/store/memory/store_test.go:836 injects a dayAdvancingClock and advances it 25 hours PER PAGE so V2-079's seven-page walk can run at all; internal/api/repositories_test.go:44-49 explains that its three tests each build a fresh handler because 'four owner reads in one store exhaust that budget'; internal/application/repository_test.go:842-846 splits one test in two for the same reason. Two of those three comments assert it is a real production property, and after this task they are false.

decisions.decision: What the in-memory adapter counts as actual usage: distinct RECORD KEYS, mirroring the Firestore document set, not rows returned and not calls made. The rule, stated so it can be checked: (a) a key counts once however many times it is read in one transaction, mirroring len(u.cache); (b) a MISS counts as one read, because the Firestore adapter caches nil for NotFound (store.go:503-505) and Firestore bills a get of a missing document; (c) a paged read counts min(limit+1, rows remaining after the cursor), because the Firestore query is Limit(limit+1) and countReads sees every snapshot it returned (store.go:657-662); (d) the quota record counts as one read and one write, because the Firestore adapter reads it through u.value (so it enters the cache) and stages it (so it enters u.values); (e) a write counts its key once per transaction, mirroring len(u.values); (f) a single-key read of a key already written in the same transaction counts nothing, mirroring u.value's short-circuit on u.values (store.go:525-530); (g) deletes stay zero on both adapters, because neither has a delete operation.
decisions.rationale: The alternative -- counting calls, or counting rows scanned -- is what would make the two adapters disagree in the other direction. Counting rows SCANNED would over-charge the memory adapter, whose RequirementsPage sorts every row (memory/store.go:208-227) while Firestore's query stops at limit+1; counting rows RETURNED would under-charge it by exactly the probe row that tells the caller whether another page exists. Clause (b) is the one most likely to be argued away and is the one Firestore actually bills. Clause (d) is not bookkeeping pedantry: the read transaction reserves 6,001 reads and 1 write, and if the memory adapter charged itself nothing for the quota record its trued-up write count would be zero where Firestore's is one, so the very first row of the cross-adapter table would disagree. Where clause (f) and the query paths cannot both be honoured -- Firestore's queries hit the server even for a key already staged -- the measurement, not the design, decides: report the divergence rather than forcing the numbers together (d5).

decisions.decision: Where it lives. internal/store/memory's unit gains a read-key set, a write-key set, and the three fields the Firestore adapter already keeps for this purpose (the reserved usage, its key, and whether a reservation happened), plus two small helpers -- one that records a read key and one that records a write key -- and a query-path helper that records several. Keys are namespaced as kind plus separator plus id, so two aggregates sharing an id are two documents exactly as they are two paths in Firestore. The true-up runs inside Store.Transact (memory/store.go:171-183) AFTER the callback returns nil and BEFORE m.data = working, which is the same position flush() gives it in the Firestore adapter; it applies to the CLONED working state, so a failed transaction drops the reservation and the true-up together, exactly as an aborted Firestore transaction does.
decisions.rationale: Placing the true-up on the clone is what keeps rollback semantics identical without a second mechanism: the memory adapter's atomicity is the clone-and-swap, so anything written into working -- reservation, correction, records -- vanishes on error. Reusing quota.Counter.TrueUp rather than writing a second correction is required by non_goals item 3 and is safe by construction: TrueUp clamps actual component-wise to [0, reserved] (internal/quota/quota.go:127-146), so the trued-up total can never exceed the worst case Reserve already admitted and can never fall below zero. internal/quota is therefore prohibited: nothing in the shared policy changes, only the adapter that was not applying it.

decisions.decision: Completeness is enforced mechanically, not by review. internal/store/memory/source_guard_test.go -- which already parses every .go file in the package with go/ast for its record-envelope guard -- gains a second guard that enumerates the method set of application.UnitOfWork by reflection over the interface type, then fails if the corresponding method on the adapter's unit does not call one of the counting helpers, with a short explicitly justified allow-list for the methods that touch no record at all.
decisions.rationale: A missed read is not a visible bug, it is a silent discount: the true-up over-credits and the memory adapter quietly charges less than Firestore for the same work, which is exactly the divergence this task exists to remove, arriving again through a method somebody adds next month. Seventy methods on unit were measured at 9a09ef8, so 'we instrumented them all' is a claim no reviewer can check by reading. Deriving the expected set from the port interface rather than from a hand-written list is what makes the guard survive the next port addition: a new UnitOfWork method that reads state and forgets to count fails this test rather than passing quietly. The guard cannot live inside a generic accessor instead, because the count has to be taken where the MATCH is known -- a filtered scan must charge for the rows Firestore's query would have returned, not for every row the map holds.

decisions.decision: Agreement between the two adapters is asserted, not asserted-about: one test name in BOTH adapter packages -- TestBothAdaptersSettleTheSameReservationForTheSameWorkload, in internal/store/memory/store_test.go and internal/store/firestore/quota_integration_test.go -- over the same workload table, each row asserting the committed daily Usage after the transaction against the SAME literal expectation written in both files. Rows: a bounded first page at page_size 1; the same page at page_size 2; a Requirement detail read; a capture mutation. If a row's two measurements disagree, the implementer stops and escalates: the number is not adjusted on either side, the row is not deleted, and the expectation is not widened into a range.
decisions.rationale: This is the concrete form of 'the two adapters do not disagree about what a reservation costs'. It is deliberately a shared literal duplicated in two files rather than a shared helper, because sharing it would need a third package and the only candidates are internal/quota (prohibited here) and a new package (a new component and a new manifest edge for a test fixture). The duplication is the same trade V2-079 made with one test name in both adapter packages, and it fails loudly in the case that matters: the two literals differing is a compile-time-visible diff, whereas a range-valued assertion would hide precisely the drift being guarded. Firestore's side must run under the emulator; a run without it skips and measures nothing (gate rule G7).

decisions.decision: Two exported inspection seams on memory.Store, mirroring the helpers the Firestore package already has for the same reason: one that reads the committed daily total for an instant (the counterpart of readQuotaRecord, firestore/quota_integration_test.go:181-199) and one that SEEDS that total directly, outside ReserveQuota (the counterpart of seedQuotaTotal, :165-179, whose own comment says it exists because a synthetic fill would otherwise be trued down to its own tiny actual cost). They follow the idiom of the file's existing exported inspectors (memory/store.go:974-1041, Requirement, Increment, Events, Outbox, Controls, Idempotency).
decisions.rationale: The seams are not convenience: without them this task silently breaks a real assertion. internal/api/api_test.go's TestQuotaExhaustionMapsTo429NotBadRequest (api_test.go:292 at 9a09ef8) fills the day's write budget by calling u.ReserveQuota inside a transaction that stages nothing, then expects the next capture to answer 429. With the true-up in place that fill is credited back to its own actual cost of about one write, and the 429 becomes a 201 -- a status code moving because of a store-adapter change, which is the exact class of accident V2-083's pin table exists to catch. The Firestore package hit this first and solved it by seeding the record directly; the memory adapter needs the same escape, and it must be exported because the test that needs it lives in package api. The api test is then edited to seed rather than to reserve, and nothing else about it changes -- not its name, not its assertion, not its subject.

decisions.decision: V2-079's workaround is removed, and the removal is part of this task rather than a follow-up. internal/store/memory/store_test.go's dayAdvancingClock (store_test.go:944-950) and the per-page advance in the Backlog cursor walk (:836 and the advanceOneDay call inside the loop) go away, and the walk runs on a single fixed injected instant -- exactly as its Firestore counterpart already does with integrationClock (firestore/store_test.go:1876). Both cursor-walk test names then hold fixture-identical clocks, and everything else in those tests stays byte-identical.
decisions.rationale: It belongs here because the workaround IS the symptom: a test that has to advance a simulated day between pages is the visible form of 'four read transactions fit in a day', and leaving it in place after the cause is gone would leave a reader unable to tell whether it is still load-bearing. Removing it is also the cheapest strong proof available: the two adapters' cursor-walk tests differing only in their clock was the measured evidence of divergence, so making the clocks identical while both tests still pass is evidence of convergence that costs no new fixture. A separate task would have to re-establish the whole context to delete four lines.

decisions.decision: The symptom is asserted directly as well, in a test whose name says the outcome: many consecutive read transactions on ONE fixed instant all succeed on the in-memory adapter, where five would have failed before. The bound is derived from the budget and the trued-up cost per read transaction, not from a round number picked for comfort, and the test asserts the committed daily total after the run is far below quota.DefaultBudget.Reads rather than merely that no error was returned.
decisions.rationale: The outcome sentence is 'a test that reads a handful of times does not exhaust a day's budget', and a walk that merely passes does not say that -- it could pass because something advanced a clock, or because the budget moved. Asserting the committed total closes both loopholes at once: a raised budget (non_goals item 1) would not change the total, and a reservation moved after the work (non_goals item 2) would leave the total unchanged only if nothing was reserved at all, which the same total exposes. Fixing the instant is what makes the assertion about the true-up rather than about the calendar.

decisions.decision: The two scar comments that this change falsifies are corrected in place, comment-only, and their tests keep their names, their structure and their fresh-handler-per-test shape: internal/api/repositories_test.go:44-49 ('four owner reads in one store exhaust that budget ... a real production property, not a test artefact') and internal/application/repository_test.go:842-846 ('each read crosses one bounded read-quota reservation ... the two together would exceed the hard daily budget the memory adapter enforces'). No assertion in either file is touched.
decisions.rationale: Both comments state as a production property something that was an unsettled reservation on one adapter only, and leaving a knowingly false explanation next to a passing test is the drift this project keeps paying for -- the next reader cannot tell whether the structure is still required. Correcting the sentences rather than restructuring the tests is the smallest honest change: the fresh-handler shape is harmless and its removal would touch assertions this task has no business touching. The cost is that a comment-only edit still moves the application and api component keys, so both get an evidence record; that is the price of not leaving a lie in the tree.

decisions.decision: What stays untouched, by design and not by omission: internal/quota (DefaultBudget, ReadTransactionUsage, MutationUsage and TrueUp are byte-unchanged -- no budget is raised and no correction is reimplemented), internal/application/service.go (the reservation still happens BEFORE the work, at service.go:131 and :148), internal/store/firestore/store.go (the reference implementation is the specification here, not a thing to adjust), and internal/api/api.go. Chain position: this task must be serialized AFTER V2-083, which holds internal/api/api_test.go, and it is the last source change before V2-080's live re-observation.
decisions.rationale: Each of the three non-goals maps to one prohibited path, which is what makes them checkable rather than aspirational: raising the budget means editing internal/quota, reserving after the work means editing internal/application/service.go, and letting the adapters disagree means editing internal/store/firestore/store.go to meet the memory adapter halfway. The ordering against V2-083 matters in one direction only: V2-083's route pin table contains the 429 quota row, so with V2-083 already merged, d6's api-test change is guarded by an assertion that fails if the 429 stops happening -- the accident this task is most likely to cause is exactly the one that pin table catches.

risks: Partial instrumentation is the failure mode with no symptom: an uncounted read makes the memory adapter cheaper than Firestore rather than making anything fail. d4's reflection-plus-AST guard is the only reason this task can claim completeness, so a guard that is weakened, allow-listed generously, or reduced to a hand-written method list removes the task's main safety property. If the guard cannot be written against the port interface, stop and escalate rather than shipping the instrumentation without it.

d2's clauses (b), (c) and (f) are the ones an implementer will be tempted to simplify away, because each of them makes the memory adapter charge itself for something it did not literally do. Simplifying any of them will show up as a disagreeing row in d5's table; the correct response is to restore the clause, not to widen the expectation.

The cross-adapter table can be made to pass dishonestly by adjusting one side's literal. If a row disagrees, the two measurements go into the evidence as measured and the task stops. A range-valued or tolerance-based expectation is a departure from the design.

TestQuotaExhaustionMapsTo429NotBadRequest will break the moment the true-up lands, and it will break by turning a 429 into a 201 -- a status code moving because of a store change. d6's seam is the fix; re-pointing the test at a stubbed error, deleting the test, or relaxing it to accept a 201 are all departures. V2-083's pin table must be green before and after.

internal/api/api_test.go is held by V2-083 (and by V2-082 before it). Running concurrently conflicts. Serialize after V2-083 and re-measure that task's pin-table rows rather than assuming they are unaffected.

The Firestore half of d5 measures nothing without the emulator: internal/store/firestore's cases skip and the package goes green. A skipped case is never a pass (gate rule G7); if the emulator cannot be started the store-firestore record is partial and the task stops.

Removing dayAdvancingClock (d7) is a test edit inside V2-079's own fixture. If the walk then fails for any reason other than the clock, the cause is the instrumentation and not the workaround: restore nothing, stop and escalate, because a walk that needs a day per page after this change means the true-up is not settling what it claims to.
